story.title: A better-sounding rewrite is not always a better correction
paragraphs: Grammatical error correction (GEC) must fix the language while preserving what the writer meant. An LLM corrector may produce a valid paraphrase that shares few words with the reference, or rewrite too much and shift the meaning; overlap scores penalize the first, and fluency-oriented scores can reward the second. In Figure 1, BLEU cannot separate over- from under-correction, and the reference-free metric SOME misses over-correction.

DSGram scores three criteria. Semantic Coherence asks whether meaning is preserved; Edit Level asks whether the changes were necessary, rather than counting edited tokens; Fluency covers grammar and natural expression. Folding grammaticality into fluency removes a redundant vote: in SOME's annotation data the two correlate at 0.89.

mechanism.title: Quality and importance are judged separately for each sentence
paragraphs: An LLM first scores the original–corrected pair on the three criteria, then judges how much each matters for this sentence: legal or medical text calls for strict Semantic Coherence and Edit Level, casual dialogue for Fluency. Importance is elicited as pairwise comparisons under the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), not as directly stated weights, so inconsistent judgments can be caught and revised.

Sentence-specific weights matter because a fixed average can hide a low score on the criterion that matters most for a given sentence. In Figure 5, the casual-dialogue pair receives its largest weight on Fluency and the formal pair on Edit Level.

evidence.title: Dynamic weighting helps most at sentence level; the scorer sets the ceiling
paragraphs: Weighting can be tested apart from scoring. Applied to human sub-scores on DSGram-Eval, the authors' human-scored set, AHP weights correlate 0.8764 with human overall ratings versus 0.8544 for equal weights, a difference the paper calls significant only at a relaxed level. On SEEDA, equal weights cost far more at sentence level than at system level (Table 3).

Component scores set the ceiling. GPT-4 correlates best with human sub-scores on all three criteria, LLaMA3-70B is weakest on Edit Level, and LLaMA models fine-tuned on GPT-4-annotated data beat five-shot prompting without approaching GPT-4 (Table 4). On SEEDA-S system-level Pearson correlation, IMPARA and SOME stay ahead of DSGram (Table 3).

reading_notes: Re-read submetric definitions, AHP procedure (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1), Figure 5, weighting validation and scorer ablations. v5 demo computes principal-eigenvector weights and CR (RI = 0.58) from reader-set pairwise judgments; Figure 5 weights and released DSGram-Eval human sub-scores are measured; the paper does not print its matrices. Released generate_weight.py indexes RI by matrix size (0.90 for 3×3), more lenient than the paper's 0.58; the page follows the paper.

demo.title: Derive the weights from pairwise judgments
demo.description: DSGram does not ask for weights directly. For each sentence pair, an LLM compares the three criteria two at a time on the 1–9 scale; the weights are the principal eigenvector of that judgment matrix, accepted only when its consistency ratio is below 0.1 (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1). Make the three judgments yourself for a sentence pair from Figure 5.
demo.note: Measured: Figure 5 weights and scores; human sub-scores and overall scores from the released DSGram-Eval annotation. Adapted: sentence pairs from Figure 5; RI = 0.58 and the CR < 0.1 rule from Section 3.2; scale wording from the released weight prompt. Computed: your weights, λmax, CI, CR and weighted scores. The paper prints GPT-4's weights but not its matrices; “Closest match to Figure 5” is our search over consistent integer judgments, which differs from the printed weights by up to 0.032 for (a) and 0.010 for (b). No model runs in this page.
